adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Mauritius (Wikipedia)
adds.summary: thin: no usable finding — the mandated Wikipedia full-text search ('transgender prisoner Mauritius', top hits incl. 'Timeline of LGBTQ history, 21st century' and 'HIV adult prevalence rate') produced no Mauritius-specific placement content, and the fetched article contains zero prison/jail/detention references: its 'Transgender rights' section covers legal gender recognition (not possible), name change via court process, hormone therapy availability in public hospitals and the group Association VISA-G, with no prisoner-placement rule, no trans custody unit and no solitary/segregation practice described. The only trans-related custody incident found in cached base-lane sources is in the US State Department 2016 country report — police arbitrarily arrested a transgender person for wearing women's clothing (slapped, threatened, released without charge) — an arrest incident, not a prison placement.

records.note: No prison-housing placement data for transgender prisoners in Mauritius was found: no birth-sex-vs-identity placement rule, no trans special unit, and no solitary/segregation practice, housing ruling or documented custody-placement case were located in the mandated Wikipedia full-text search plus the lane's candidate fetches (cached base-lane sources — Outright International MUS page, AfricLaw, Young Queer Alliance brief, State Dept 2016 — were also checked and contain no placement content). Mauritius' legal-gender-recognition gap (no recognition possible) means official records would not reflect a trans person's identity, but no citable source documents actual custody placement, so the honest result is: no usable placement finding.

adds.title: Senegal | Outright International
adds.summary: Outright International's Senegal overview (last updated 12 March 2026) documents the criminal-law framework that lands LGBT people in Senegalese custody but contains no trans-specific housing placement: a law approved by parliament in March 2026 and signed by the President on 27 March 2026 raises Article 319 'acts against nature' prison terms to five to ten years, criminalizes being transgender, and criminalizes the 'promotion of homosexuality'. Documented enforcement: in December 2025 police arrested 15 people who shared a WhatsApp group, subjecting them to forced anal examinations (described as a form of torture); a court convicted six of 'indecent exposure, indecent acts, and criminal conspiracy' and four remained in pretrial detention as of December 2025, with further arrests in February 2026. The page gives no description of where convicted trans prisoners are housed (birth-sex vs identity placement), no trans special unit, and no solitary/segregation practice, and states there is no formal recognition of trans or intersex people in Senegal.

adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Senegal (Wikipedia)
adds.summary: The mandated Wikipedia full-text search ('transgender prisoner Senegal') returned no placement-specific article, and the fetched 'LGBTQ rights in Senegal' article documents only prosecution and sentencing, never housing placement: on 19 December 2008 nine men were arrested in a Dakar flat (including Diadji Diouf of AIDES Senegal), tortured in police custody, and on 6 January 2009 convicted of 'indecent conduct and unnatural acts' (5 years) and criminal-group membership (3 years); in October 2012 a Dakar court sentenced Tasmir Jupiter Ndiaye to four years and a 200,000 CFA fine for 'acts against nature' plus illegal arms and battery charges (his complainant Matar Diop got three years); arrest waves followed in 2018 and February 2026 (22 men in two weeks, including TikToker Saliou Mbaye 'Zale', arrested 20 February 2026 at the Senegal–Gambia border), and in August 2026 police arrested 99 men on same-sex-activity charges, releasing 28, with 71 facing up to 20 years after penalties were doubled. These are criminalisation/sentencing records; the article contains no information on where prisoners are housed, no trans-specific placement rule or unit, and no solitary/segregation practice for trans prisoners.

records.note: No trans-prisoner housing-placement data for Senegal was found: no birth-sex-vs-identity placement rule, no trans special unit, and no solitary/segregation or in-prison housing practice for trans prisoners were located in the mandated Wikipedia search plus the lane's fetches. What is documented is the criminalisation framework driving detention — Article 319 'acts against nature' enforcement with dated conviction cases (9 men convicted 6 Jan 2009 in Dakar to 5+3 years; October 2012 Dakar sentence of Tasmir Jupiter Ndiaye to four years; 2018 and February 2026 arrest waves; 99 men arrested in August 2026, 71 facing up to 20 years) and the March 2026 law (signed 27 March 2026) raising same-sex-act terms to five-to-ten years while criminalizing being transgender — but none of these sources describes where trans prisoners are housed, so the honest result is: no usable placement finding.
